reason: The sources provide over 10 cross-verified claims from multiple independent websites regarding solar physics, mass calculations, solar shape, and heliospheric dynamics.
story: To measure the Sun, humanity first had to weigh the Earth. In 1798, Henry Cavendish used a delicate torsion balance to determine the gravitational constant, giving scientists the key tool to calculate planetary and solar masses using Isaac Newton's laws. Applying these principles revealed that the Sun dominates our entire cosmic neighborhood, driving the Solar System with its immense gravity. Deep inside its core, nuclear fusion transforms hydrogen into helium, primarily via the proton-proton chain which supplies about 99 percent of its power, alongside a tiny contribution from the CNO cycle. Beyond its power output, observations by NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory show that the Sun is the closest thing to a perfect sphere ever observed in nature, maintaining its shape throughout intense 11-year magnetic cycles. Meanwhile, its solar wind carves out the heliosphere, a massive magnetic shield protecting our cosmic home from interstellar radiation.
angle: The Sun is the closest natural object to a perfect sphere ever observed, holding a constant shape that refuses to bulge or distort even during intense 11-year solar magnetic storms.

claims.claim: Hydrogen fusion in the solar core converts hydrogen into helium to power the Sun.
The proton-proton (pp) chain reaction generates approximately 99 percent of the Sun's total energy.
The CNO fusion cycle contributes around 1 percent (or 0.8 percent) of the total energy produced by the Sun.
Henry Cavendish measured the gravitational constant in 1798 using a torsion balance experiment.
Isaac Newton used universal gravitation principles to mathematically determine solar and planetary mass relationships.
The Solar Dynamics Observatory measured the precise oblateness and shape of the Sun from space.
The Sun's oblate shape remains constant and does not vary with the 11-year solar activity cycle.
The Sun is considered the natural object closest to a perfect sphere ever observed.
The heliosphere is a protective bubble created by the solar wind that shields the Solar System from interstellar gas and cosmic rays.
The Voyager 1 spacecraft traveled to the outer region of the heliosphere to study the solar wind boundary.
The solar wind is a continuous outflow of magnetized plasma and particles emitted by the Sun into space.
The mass of celestial bodies can be calculated using Newton's laws by analyzing gravitational interactions and orbital motions.

disputed: Exact percentage of CNO cycle energy contribution: S2 cites 0.8% while S5 cites 'of the order of 1 per cent'. Script should state 'around 1 percent'.

Voyager 1 heliosphere status: S4 (from 2005) notes Voyager 1 approaching the termination shock at 94 AU, whereas S2 (modern) confirms it entered the interstellar medium in August 2012 at 122 AU. Script should use the confirmed crossing.
